Multi-season models follow the same sites through several seasons, and ask how occupancy
changes between them. This vignette uses [project 0010](https://raid.org/10.83062/9eec588a),
shipped with WildObsR: 28 camera stations in Woomargama National Park, New South Wales, that
ran almost continuously for ten months in 2021–22. It builds on *Detection histories and sampling
effort* and *Fit single-season models*.

## How WildObs splits a long survey

WildObs data curation for the database involves spliting long-term sampling into single-season surveys,
its `deploymentGroups`, of at most 100 days, so each can be modelled as one closed season. The WildObsR
function `survey_and_deployment_generator()` is the function that defines them from the timing of the 
records. Here it rebuilds 0010's surveys from its observations:


``` r
# load the R package
library(WildObsR)      # for data access and wrangling 
library(unmarked)      # for multi-season occupancy models
library(spOccupancy)   # for bayesian multi-season occupancy models 

# grab the Woomargama project shipped with WildObsR
dp <- example_datapackages("NSW_Woomargama_wombats_Linley_2021-22_WildObsID_0010")[[1]]
# extract the deployments and observations, read with their schema types
deps <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "deployments")
obs <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "observations")

# remove obscured observations
caps <- obs[!grepl("^obscured_for_", obs$deploymentID), ]
# merge locationName (the project's landscape) to observations via deploymentID
caps <- merge(caps, deps[, c("deploymentID", "locationName")], by = "deploymentID")

# save the dataSource for survey generator (required for overlapping surveys from diffent sources)
caps$dataSource <- dp$name
# since there were obscured deployments in observations that we removed, we need to 
# ensure deploymentIDs match across both tables. Thin deployments to matching records. 
deps_rec <- deps[deps$deploymentID %in% caps$deploymentID, ]

# group the records into surveys of at most 100 days (default settings)
caps <- survey_and_deployment_generator(caps, deps_rec)

# look up the deploymentGroups (surveys) WildObs recorded for each record's deployment
recorded <- deps$deploymentGroups[match(caps$deploymentID, deps$deploymentID)]
# compile the records in each rebuilt survey, beside the survey WildObs recorded
table(rebuilt = caps$new_deploymentGroups, recorded = sub("_Linley.*", "", recorded))
#>                               recorded
#> rebuilt                        Woomargama_NP_2021_a Woomargama_NP_2021_b
#>   Woomargama_NP_2021_a_2021-22                 5246                    0
#>   Woomargama_NP_2021_b_2021-22                    0                 6383
#>   Woomargama_NP_2022_a_2021-22                    0                    0
#>   Woomargama_NP_2022_b_2021-22                    0                    0
#>                               recorded
#> rebuilt                        Woomargama_NP_2022_a Woomargama_NP_2022_b
#>   Woomargama_NP_2021_a_2021-22                    0                    0
#>   Woomargama_NP_2021_b_2021-22                    0                    0
#>   Woomargama_NP_2022_a_2021-22                 5138                    0
#>   Woomargama_NP_2022_b_2021-22                    0                  216
```

The rebuilt surveys match the four recorded ones. The data package already holds them, so you
rarely need to run this yourself. You can inspect the start and stop dates of each survey in 
the metadata:


``` r
# grab the start and end of each survey, from the temporal metadata
blocks <- dp$temporal[grepl("WildObsID", names(dp$temporal))]
# compile into a table for display 
data.frame(survey = names(blocks), start = sapply(blocks, `[[`, "start"),
           end = sapply(blocks, `[[`, "end"), row.names = NULL)
#>                                       survey      start        end
#> 1 Woomargama_NP_2021_a_Linley_WildObsID_0010 2021-06-27 2021-10-05
#> 2 Woomargama_NP_2021_b_Linley_WildObsID_0010 2021-10-05 2022-01-13
#> 3 Woomargama_NP_2022_a_Linley_WildObsID_0010 2022-01-13 2022-04-23
#> 4 Woomargama_NP_2022_b_Linley_WildObsID_0010 2022-04-23 2022-04-28

# and calculate the total duration (in days) from overall start and stop dates, including the start date (+1)
total_dur <- as.numeric(difftime(dp$temporal$end, dp$temporal$start, units = "days")) + 1
total_dur
#> [1] 306
```

Notice the end date of a prior survey shares the start date of the next survey, 
indicating that the continuous sampling was split into 100-day blocks. The fourth
survey lasted only a few days, so we will need to link this shorter season to the 
prior season when preparing for the analyis. 

## Rebuild long-term deployments

Because surveys end at 100 days, a camera that ran for ten months appears as several
deployments. The WildObsR function `recombine_deployment_groups()` joins them back 
into one deployment per camera location within each `multiSeason_deploymentGroup`, and 
keeps a crosswalk to the original 100-day deployments (*i.e.*, pieces):


``` r
# remake the data pacakge to one deployment per camera per multi-season group
dp_long <- recombine_deployment_groups(dp)
#> NSW_Woomargama_wombats_Linley_2021-22_WildObsID_0010: 94 obscured observations row(s) kept unchanged in recombine_deployment_groups(); they have no camera to join to.

# extract the rebuilt deployments, and the crosswalk to the original pieces
deps_long <- frictionless::read_resource(dp_long, "deployments")
crosswalk <- frictionless::read_resource(dp_long, "deployment_crosswalk")
# also extract the observations, now pointing at the rebuilt deployments
obs_long <- frictionless::read_resource(dp_long, "observations")

# compare the number of deployments before and after
c(original = nrow(deps), rebuilt = nrow(deps_long))
#> original  rebuilt 
#>      219       57

# confirm the locationIDs remain unchanged from the 100-day deployments
setdiff(deps$locationID, deps_long$locationID); setdiff(deps_long$locationID, deps$locationID)
#> character(0)
#> character(0)
```

## Effort on a shared calendar

A multi-season model needs occasion `k` to cover the same dates at every site, so the 
`align = "calendar"` parameter in the WildObsR `effort_matrix()` function starts every 
station's occasions on the first day of the project. The crosswalk takes effort from 
the original pieces, so any gap between them counts as no effort. 

We will be modelling three seasons by combining the last short season to the prior season.
Therefore, we will fold in the extra 6 days of sampling duration into the last season, which
makes that season slightly longer than the rest. 

When we use 10-day occasions over the 306 days, we produce 10 occassions for each season, 
plus an extra 11th occasion for the last season with reduced sampling effort in that occasion"


``` r
# create the effort matrix using the locationID as the sampling location and specifying occasion length + duration
eff <- effort_matrix(deps_long, site_col = "locationID", w = 10, dur = total_dur,
                     # ensure detections are aligned thru calendar, and provide the recombination crosswalk 
                     align = "calendar", crosswalk = crosswalk,
                     # specify the project's timezone 
                     time_zone = dp$temporal$timeZone)

# grab the start date of every occasion
occ_start <- unique(eff$occasions[, c("occasion", "start")])$start
# define the survey each occasion starts in: the last survey that began on or before it
season <- vapply(occ_start, function(s) {
  # the surveys that had begun by this date
  begun <- vapply(blocks, function(b) as.Date(b$start) <= s, logical(1))
  # take the latest of them
  names(blocks)[max(which(begun))]
}, character(1))
# fold the five-day fourth survey into the third season
season[season == names(blocks)[4]] <- names(blocks)[3]

# view how many occasions each season holds
table(season)
#> season
#> Woomargama_NP_2021_a_Linley_WildObsID_0010 
#>                                         10 
#> Woomargama_NP_2021_b_Linley_WildObsID_0010 
#>                                         10 
#> Woomargama_NP_2022_a_Linley_WildObsID_0010
#>                                         11
```

## Covariates that change each season

Recombining 100-day deployments into multi-season deployments averages each covariate over a 
camera's entire duration, so covariates that measure weather that changes between seasons is 
lost. The original `covariates` table has one row per 100-day deployment, with its station and 
survey, so covariates that change each season come from there instead:


``` r
# grab the covariates of the original 100-day deployments, each with its station and survey
covs <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "covariates")
# leave out the five-day fourth survey, so its short window does not skew the third season
covs <- covs[covs$deploymentGroups != names(blocks)[4], ]

## extract rainfall and temperature covariates by averaging values in each survey: station x season
rain <- tapply(covs$mean_monthly_precipitation_point, list(covs$locationID, covs$deploymentGroups), mean)
temp <- tapply(covs$mean_monthly_temperature_point, list(covs$locationID, covs$deploymentGroups), mean)
# order the stations and seasons to match the effort matrix
rain <- rain[rownames(eff$effort), unique(season)]
temp <- temp[rownames(eff$effort), unique(season)]

# view the mean monthly temperature of the first three stations in each season
round(head(temp, 3), 1)
#>                   Woomargama_NP_2021_a_Linley_WildObsID_0010
#> 1_WildObsID_0010                                         6.5
#> 10_WildObsID_0010                                        7.5
#> 11_WildObsID_0010                                        7.4
#>                   Woomargama_NP_2021_b_Linley_WildObsID_0010
#> 1_WildObsID_0010                                        11.2
#> 10_WildObsID_0010                                       12.5
#> 11_WildObsID_0010                                       12.4
#>                   Woomargama_NP_2022_a_Linley_WildObsID_0010
#> 1_WildObsID_0010                                        21.4
#> 10_WildObsID_0010                                       22.7
#> 11_WildObsID_0010                                       22.6

# we can also prepare a static covariate that does not vary across seasons, like altitude
# aggregate one altitude per station via the mean of its deployments
elev <- aggregate(altitude_point ~ locationID, data = covs, FUN = mean)
# view the first few stations
head(elev, 3)

```

## Colonisation and extinction in unmarked

The black rat (*Rattus rattus*), an introduced species, was detected at multiple stations across
each season. The function `colext()` from unmarked estimates the occupancy of the first season, 
then the probability that an empty station is colonised and that an occupied one goes extinct 
between seasons. It also allows us to include both covariates that vary in space (`siteCovs`), 
covariates that vary between seasons (`yearlySiteCovs`), and detection-level covariates that vary
per occasion (`obsCovs`):


``` r
# create the detection history of black rats in each station and occasion, and include 
y_rat <- detection_matrix(obs = obs_long, effort = eff, scientificNames = "Rattus rattus", type = "occupancy")
#> detection_matrix(): set aside 94 obscured observation(s), which carry no camera.
#> Detection histories from public data under-count those species where they are listed.

# format the matrix for unmarked, using one site covariate for elevation
umf <- model_matrix_input(detections = y_rat, effort = eff, site_covs = elev,
                          # and specifying the season of every occasion
                          seasons = season, output = "unmarked")
# add the covariates that change each season, one row per station and season, station by station
unmarked::yearlySiteCovs(umf) <- data.frame(rain = as.vector(t(rain)), temp = as.vector(t(temp)))

# view the number of stations, seasons and occasions in total
c(stations = unmarked::numSites(umf), seasons = umf@numPrimary, occasions = ncol(unmarked::getY(umf)))
#>  stations   seasons occasions 
#>        28         3        33
```

In addition to the occupancy formula (`psiformula`) and detection probability formula 
(`pformula`) that is shared with a single-season occupancy model, `colext()` adds additional
parameters for colonization probability (`gammaformula`) and extinction probability 
(`epsilonformula`) from one season to the next. Another departure from the single-season 
occupancy model is that `psiformula` describes occupancy in the *first season only*. 

``` r
# fit the multi-season occupancy model, where altitude affects the first season
rat_colext <- colext(psiformula = ~ scale(altitude_point), 
                     # rainfall affects colonization, temps affect extinction
                     gammaformula = ~ scale(rain), epsilonformula = ~ scale(temp),
                     # and assume detection probability rises with effort. 
                     pformula = ~ scale(effort), data = umf)
# view the model results
rat_colext
#> 
#> Call:
#> colext(psiformula = ~altitude_point, gammaformula = ~rain, epsilonformula = ~temp, 
#>     pformula = ~scale(effort), data = umf)
#> 
#> Initial (logit-scale):
#>                 Estimate      SE      z P(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)    -0.098605 2.29298 -0.043   0.966
#> altitude_point  0.000609 0.00359  0.170   0.865
#> 
#> Colonization (logit-scale):
#>             Estimate     SE     z P(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)   2.5014 1.5321  1.63   0.103
#> rain         -0.0181 0.0131 -1.38   0.168
#> 
#> Extinction (logit-scale):
#>             Estimate    SE      z P(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)    0.589 1.719  0.343   0.732
#> temp          -0.240 0.197 -1.222   0.222
#> 
#> Detection (logit-scale):
#>               Estimate     SE      z P(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)    -0.0945 0.0823 -1.149   0.251
#> scale(effort)  -0.0752 0.0785 -0.958   0.338
#> 
#> AIC: 939.0988 
#> Number of sites: 28

# the share of stations occupied in each season, for the population and for these 28 stations
rbind(population = rat_colext@projected.mean["occupied", ],
      these_stations = smoothed(rat_colext)["occupied", ])
#>                        1         2         3
#> population     0.5723576 0.6402964 0.8627115
#> these_stations 0.5723484 0.6439193 0.8577212
```

Occupancy rose from winter 2021 to summer 2022 because colonisation strongly 
outweighed extinction (as indicated by each parameter's intercept). We can also see
that the covariates included for the analysis did not have a significant (`P(>|z|)` 
< 0.05) affect on any of the parameters specified, as these covariates were used only
for illustrative purposes. 

## Occupancy over time in spOccupancy

The function `tPGOcc()` from the spOccupancy package models occupancy in each season directly,
here as a trend across the seasons, rather than through colonisation and extinction. Its `y` 
is station x season x occasion:


``` r
# format the detections for spOccupancy, with site covariates and a season dimension
rat_sp <- model_matrix_input(y_rat, eff, site_covs = elev, seasons = season, output = "spOccupancy")
# view station x season x occasion dimensions
dim(rat_sp$y)
#> [1] 28  3 11

# the number of stations
n_station <- nrow(rat_sp$y)
# make the occupancy covariates a list, so covariates that change each season can join elevation
rat_sp$occ.covs <- as.list(rat_sp$occ.covs)
# add the season of every station as a matrix besides the list 
rat_sp$occ.covs$season <- matrix(1:3, n_station, 3, byrow = TRUE)
# add the station x season covariates
rat_sp$occ.covs$rain <- rain
rat_sp$occ.covs$temp <- temp
# the season of every station, season and occasion, for detection
rat_sp$det.covs$season <- array(rep(1:3, each = n_station), dim = dim(rat_sp$y))
# number each station, for a random intercept in detection
rat_sp$det.covs$station <- seq_len(n_station)
```

Note that unlike unmarked, `tPGOcc()` has no colonization or extinction parameters. Instead, 
it models occupancy in each season directly, though you can linke neighbouring season through
a temporal random effect by specifying the parameter `ar1 = TRUE`. For our model, we include 
each occupancy covariate from the unmarked model in the `occ.formula` parameter in `tPGOcc()`. 
We assume differ among stations and among seasons, so we have added a random intercept term 
to the detection formula for each station and a fixed effect for each season:

``` r
# make the chains repeatable
set.seed(1)
# a trend in occupancy across seasons; detection by effort, season and station
# fit the multi-season model including covariates affecting occupancy, 
rat_t <- tPGOcc(occ.formula = ~  scale(altitude_point) + scale(rain) + scale(temp),
                # covariates and random effect affecting detection
                det.formula = ~ scale(effort) + factor(season) + (1 | station),
                # and specify the data source and MCMC settings 
                data = rat_sp, n.batch = 600, batch.length = 25, n.burn = 5000,
                n.thin = 10, n.chains = 3, verbose = FALSE)
# view the results 
summary(rat_t)
#> 
#> Call:
#> tPGOcc(occ.formula = ~season, det.formula = ~scale(effort) + 
#>     factor(season) + (1 | station), data = rat_sp, n.batch = 600, 
#>     batch.length = 25, verbose = FALSE, n.burn = 5000, n.thin = 10, 
#>     n.chains = 3)
#> 
#> Samples per Chain: 15000
#> Burn-in: 5000
#> Thinning Rate: 10
#> Number of Chains: 3
#> Total Posterior Samples: 3000
#> Run Time (min): 0.1746
#> 
#> Occurrence (logit scale): 
#>               Mean     SD    2.5%    50%  97.5%   Rhat  ESS
#> (Intercept) 0.7426 1.2851 -1.6564 0.6910 3.5063 1.0039 2513
#> season      1.5611 1.0061  0.0013 1.4185 3.9448 1.0212  489
#> 
#> Detection (logit scale): 
#>                    Mean     SD    2.5%     50%   97.5%   Rhat  ESS
#> (Intercept)     -1.5143 0.4870 -2.4665 -1.5214 -0.5808 1.0073  639
#> scale(effort)   -0.0459 0.1065 -0.2576 -0.0470  0.1634 1.0016 3184
#> factor(season)2  0.1734 0.2843 -0.3750  0.1737  0.7198 1.0017 2827
#> factor(season)3  1.4211 0.2938  0.8656  1.4172  1.9874 1.0020 2466
#> 
#> Detection Random Effect Variances (logit scale): 
#>           Mean     SD   2.5%    50%   97.5%   Rhat  ESS
#> station 5.3901 2.0702 2.5394 5.0162 10.4357 1.0001 2091
```

Like our single-season models, spOccupancy offers model goodness-of-fit tests
through the `ppcOcc()` function that computes a posterior predictive check. We
have specified the Freeman-Tukey as the relevant test statistic for this model: 

``` r
# compare real and simulated detections, summed by station, then by occasion
summary(ppcOcc(rat_t, fit.stat = "freeman-tukey", group = 1))
#> Currently on time period 1 out of 3
#> Currently on time period 2 out of 3
#> Currently on time period 3 out of 3
#> 
#> Call:
#> ppcOcc(object = rat_t, fit.stat = "freeman-tukey", group = 1)
#> 
#> Samples per Chain: 15000
#> Burn-in: 5000
#> Thinning Rate: 10
#> Number of Chains: 3
#> Total Posterior Samples: 3000
#> 
#> ----------------------------------------
#> 	All time periods combined
#> ----------------------------------------
#> Bayesian p-value:  0.1436 
#> 
#> ----------------------------------------
#> 	Individual time periods
#> ----------------------------------------
#> Time Period 1 Bayesian p-value: 0.1073
#> Time Period 2 Bayesian p-value: 0.1053
#> Time Period 3 Bayesian p-value: 0.218
#> Fit statistic:  freeman-tukey

# repeat goodness of fit measured across all occasions
summary(ppcOcc(rat_t, fit.stat = "freeman-tukey", group = 2))
#> Currently on time period 1 out of 3
#> Currently on time period 2 out of 3
#> Currently on time period 3 out of 3
#> 
#> Call:
#> ppcOcc(object = rat_t, fit.stat = "freeman-tukey", group = 2)
#> 
#> Samples per Chain: 15000
#> Burn-in: 5000
#> Thinning Rate: 10
#> Number of Chains: 3
#> Total Posterior Samples: 3000
#> 
#> ----------------------------------------
#> 	All time periods combined
#> ----------------------------------------
#> Bayesian p-value:  0.2041 
#> 
#> ----------------------------------------
#> 	Individual time periods
#> ----------------------------------------
#> Time Period 1 Bayesian p-value: 0.2747
#> Time Period 2 Bayesian p-value: 0.3043
#> Time Period 3 Bayesian p-value: 0.0333
#> Fit statistic:  freeman-tukey
```

The chains converge and occupancy rises across the seasons, as `colext()` found. The model 
similarly reports no clear (i.e., 95% credible interval does not overlap zero) effects from
any covariate, mirroring the results from unmarked. The Bayesian p-values, though, fall below
the 0.25 to 0.75 we treat as an adequate fit, so this model still misses some of the variation
in detection. Before trusting its estimates, try detection covariates that change within a 
season, or a random effect for each station in each season. With 28 stations,  simpler models 
may also suit the data better.
